title: A Prayer for Guidance and Mercy
overview: A person under pressure from enemies and weighed down by past wrongs asks God to guide them, forgive them and keep them safe.

parts.label: Trusting and not disgraced (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: In Hebrew this psalm is an alphabet poem, each verse starting with the next letter, though the pattern has a few gaps. The writer stakes everything on God and asks not to be 'put to shame,' meaning publicly humiliated when a hope collapses, while those who betray others for no reason are the ones who should end up disgraced.

parts.label: Asking to be taught (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: The writer asks God to show them the right way to live, saying their hope rests on him all day long. They ask God to remember his long record of kindness rather than the wrongs of their youth, leaning on God's goodness instead of their own.

parts.label: What the LORD is like (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Because God is good and fair, he teaches people who have gone wrong and guides those humble enough to listen, staying loving and faithful to those who keep his covenant, the binding agreement between God and Israel. In the middle of this praise the writer breaks in to ask forgiveness, saying the wrong is great and so pardon is needed all the more.

parts.label: Those who honor God (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: People who 'fear the LORD,' meaning they hold him in deep respect, are promised guidance, a settled life and a future in the land God promised Israel's ancestors. God shares his mind with them like a close friend, and the writer keeps looking to him to free their feet from the trap, a hunter's image for enemies' schemes.

parts.label: Lonely and surrounded (vv. 16-21)
parts.note: The tone turns raw: the writer feels alone, overwhelmed by inner troubles, burdened by sin and hated fiercely by many enemies. They ask God to protect them and let their honest, upright life guard them, though a few readers take 'integrity and uprightness' to mean God's own faithfulness.

parts.label: A prayer for all Israel (v. 22)
parts.note: The last line widens the prayer from one person to the whole nation. It falls outside the alphabet pattern, so many scholars think it was added later when the psalm came into shared worship.

think: When you look back on mistakes from your younger years, what would it take for you to feel they no longer define who you are?
